Key: dark circle with label, an ion; mid-size orange circle, oxygen atom; small white circle, hydrogen atom.

items.q: When the barrier is removed, the gas changes from Box X to Box Y. Which statement correctly gives the sign of the change in entropy and the particle-level reason?
options: ΔS > 0: the atoms look messier once the barrier is gone, and a messier gas is a more disordered gas.
ΔS > 0: each atom can now be anywhere in twice the volume, so there are more possible arrangements (microstates).
ΔS < 0: the atoms are farther apart in Box Y, so they attract each other less and hold less energy.
ΔS = 0: no bonds form or break and the temperature stays constant, so nothing about the gas has changed at the particle level.

items.q: The atoms in Box Y combine to form the molecules in Box Z, at the same temperature and volume. What is the sign of the change in entropy?
options: Positive: each A₂ molecule is larger than an atom and so takes up more of the space.
Zero: the number of A atoms is the same in both boxes, so the entropy of the gas is the same too.
Positive: forming bonds releases energy, and the released energy spreads into the surroundings.
Negative: eight independent particles become four, so there are fewer ways to arrange them.

items.q: The gas in Box Y is heated from 300 K to 400 K at constant volume. What happens to its entropy, and why?
options: It increases: the atoms have a wider range of speeds, so the energy can be shared in more ways.
It stays the same: the volume and the number of atoms do not change, and those two alone decide entropy.
It decreases: faster atoms spend less time in each spot, so each atom has fewer positions on average.
It increases: the heated atoms expand, so each atom becomes bigger and fills more of the box.

items.q: Which changes to the gas in Box Y would increase its entropy? Select ALL that apply.
options: Letting it expand into a container twice as large at the same temperature
Warming it from 300 K to 350 K in the same container
Compressing it into half the volume at the same temperature
Cooling it from 300 K to 250 K in the same container
Letting the atoms pair up to form A₂ molecules, as in Box Z

items.q: For which processes is the change in entropy of the system negative? Select ALL that apply.
options: P1
P2
P3
P4
P5

items.q: Which is the best justification for the sign of the change in entropy in P2?
options: It is positive: the reaction breaks one compound into two, and breaking things apart makes a system more disordered.
It is negative: CaO(s) is a more compact solid than CaCO₃(s), so its ions have fewer places to be in the crystal.
It is positive: a mole of gas forms from a solid, and gas particles move freely through a far larger volume.
It is positive: the reaction absorbs heat, and any reaction that absorbs heat gains entropy.

items.q: In P1, ice melts at 0 °C. Which statement describes what happens to the water molecules?
options: They speed up a great deal, because the temperature of the water rises while the ice melts.
They break their O–H covalent bonds, so each molecule comes apart into separate atoms.
They leave fixed positions in the crystal and can slide past one another.
They end up farther apart than in steam, which spreads the matter out even more.

items.q: A student says P5 must lower the entropy, because water molecules line up around each ion. Which reply is best?
options: Water is held around the ions, but the ions spreading through the solution has the larger effect, so ΔS > 0.
Water molecules are not attracted to ions, so the ions spread out freely and the entropy of the water stays unchanged.
Dissolving is a physical change rather than a chemical reaction, so the entropy of the system stays the same.
The student is right: the lining up of water molecules around the ions outweighs the spreading of the ions.

items.q: What does the entropy of a system measure?
options: How much heat it releases when it reacts with oxygen
How messy the system looks in a particle drawing of its contents
The average kinetic energy of its particles
The number of ways its particles and energy can be arranged

items.q: Which has the greater entropy: 1 mol of liquid water at 100 °C or 1 mol of steam at 100 °C?
options: The liquid, because its molecules are packed closely and collide more often
The steam, because its molecules spread through the whole container
They are equal, because the substance, amount and temperature are the same
The liquid, because hydrogen bonds hold more energy than a gas does

items.q: On a cold morning, water vapor condenses into droplets on a window. Which other process has the same sign of change in entropy for the substance involved?
options: Liquid bromine freezing to a solid
Dry ice, solid CO₂, turning straight to gas
Sugar dissolving in a cup of tea
A puddle of water evaporating

items.q: Which reaction has a positive change in entropy?
options: 2 NO(g) + O₂(g) → 2 NO₂(g)
2 NO₂(g) → N₂O₄(g)
2 NO₂(g) → 2 NO(g) + O₂(g)
NH₃(g) + HCl(g) → NH₄Cl(s)

items.q: At the same temperature and pressure, 1 mol of argon gas has less entropy than 1 mol of propane gas, C₃H₈. Which is the best explanation?
options: Propane has the larger molar mass, and the entropy of a gas is set by the mass of each mole of it.
A propane molecule has more atoms, so it can store energy in more ways by rotating and vibrating.
Argon atoms are more disordered than propane molecules because each argon atom is much smaller.
Propane molecules attract one another more strongly, so they spread out through more of the space.

items.q: Predict how the entropy of the system changes in each case.

variables.name: A sealed flask of helium is connected to an empty flask of the same size at the same temperature
A cup of hot coffee cools from 70 °C to 40 °C (entropy of the coffee)
A copper block at 25 °C is moved from one shelf to another at 25 °C
Solid iodine sublimes to iodine gas

items.q: Two students explain why the entropy of water decreases when it freezes. Student 1: "The ice is more ordered." Student 2: "In ice the molecules are held in fixed positions in a lattice, so there are fewer arrangements of the molecules and their energy." Which evaluation is correct?
options: Student 1 alone is right, because entropy is defined as the amount of disorder in a system.
Both are wrong, because the entropy of the water increases when the liquid freezes into a solid lattice.
Both are equally complete, since "ordered" and "fewer arrangements" mean the same thing.
Both give the right sign; Student 2 also gives the particle-level reason (fewer arrangements).

items.q: A drop of food coloring spreads through a glass of still water over an hour, at constant temperature. What happens to the entropy of the dye molecules?
options: It decreases, because the dye becomes harder to see once it spreads
It stays the same, because no heat is added and the temperature is constant
It decreases, because the water molecules push the dye molecules apart
It increases, because each dye molecule can now be anywhere in the glass

items.q: Calculate ΔS° for the reaction N₂(g) + 3 H₂(g) → 2 NH₃(g).

mistakes.why: Value: you left out the coefficients. Multiply each S° by its coefficient: 2 for NH₃ and 3 for H₂.
Value: you used the coefficient for NH₃ but not the 3 for H₂.
Units: the table is in J/(mol·K), so the answer is in J/(mol·K) unless you convert on purpose.

items.q: Calculate ΔS° for the combustion of methane at 298 K: CH₄(g) + 2 O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2 H₂O(l).

mistakes.why: Value: you used S° for H₂O(g). The equation makes liquid water, so use 69.9 J/(mol·K).
Value: you left out the coefficients of 2 on H₂O and O₂.

items.q: If the water in the combustion of methane were formed as a gas instead of a liquid, ΔS° would be −5.3 J/(mol·K) instead of −243.1 J/(mol·K). Which statement explains the difference?
options: Making a gas releases less heat, and less heat released means more entropy for the products.
Gaseous water molecules spread through the whole container, so H₂O(g) has far more microstates.
The version that makes water vapor has fewer moles of products, so its ΔS° is closer to zero.
H₂O(g) has a larger molar mass than H₂O(l), so each mole of the gas carries more entropy.

items.q: Calculate ΔS° for the vaporization of one mole of water at 298 K, H₂O(l) → H₂O(g).
Using your answer for N₂(g) + 3 H₂(g) → 2 NH₃(g), calculate ΔS° for 4 NH₃(g) → 2 N₂(g) + 6 H₂(g).

mistakes.why: Value: you reversed the reaction but did not double it. ΔS° is extensive: twice the amount of reaction, twice the entropy change.
Value: you doubled ΔS° but kept its sign. Reversing a reaction flips the sign of ΔS°.

items.q: Why is the entropy of Q zero at 0 K?
options: At 0 K the substance has no mass left, so there is nothing to have entropy.
Entropy is set to zero for any pure substance in its standard state, as ΔH°f is for elements.
At 0 K the particles move fastest, so they spend no time at any single place in the crystal.
A perfect crystal at 0 K has one arrangement of its particles and energy: a single microstate.

items.q: Use the graph to find the entropy change when one mole of Q boils at 320 K.

mistakes.why: Value: that is the jump at the melting point (200 K). Boiling is the jump at 320 K.
Value: that is the entropy of the gas at 320 K. The change is the height of the jump, final minus initial.

items.q: The jump in entropy at the boiling point is much larger than the jump at the melting point. Which is the best explanation?
options: On boiling, particles go from touching to filling the whole container: a far larger gain in arrangements than melting gives.
Boiling happens at the higher temperature, and a higher temperature gives a larger jump for any phase change of Q.
Boiling breaks the covalent bonds inside the particles of Q, while melting leaves those bonds intact.
The gas is more disordered than the liquid, while the solid and the liquid are about equally disordered.

items.q: Between 250 K and 300 K, Q stays a liquid but its entropy still rises. Why?
options: Some of the liquid freezes as it is heated, adding solid particles to the sample of Q.
The liquid particles lose energy as they are heated, so they end up more spread out.
Their energy spreads over a wider range of speeds, giving more ways to share it.
The number of moles of Q in the sample increases as the liquid warms up.

items.q: Which statement about standard molar entropies at 298 K is correct?
options: Elements in their standard states have S° = 0, just as they have ΔH°f = 0.
Solids have negative S° values, liquids have zero, and gases have positive S° values.
Every pure substance, elements in their standard states included, has S° > 0.
S° is given in kJ/mol, the same energy unit as ΔH°f values are.

items.q: Without a table, which substance has the largest standard molar entropy at 298 K?
options: C₂H₆(g)
C(s, diamond)
H₂O(l)
CH₄(g)

items.q: For 2 NO(g) + O₂(g) → 2 NO₂(g), ΔS° = −146.6 J/(mol·K). S° is 210.8 J/(mol·K) for NO(g) and 205.2 J/(mol·K) for O₂(g). Calculate S° of NO₂(g).

mistakes.why: Value: that is the total for 2 mol of NO₂. Divide by the coefficient 2 to get S° for one mole.
Value: check the sign of ΔS°. Rearranging 2S°(NO₂) − 626.8 = −146.6 gives 2S°(NO₂) = 480.2.

items.q: Calculate ΔS° for CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g). S° values in J/(mol·K): CaCO₃(s) 91.7, CaO(s) 38.1, CO₂(g) 213.8.

mistakes.why: Sign: you subtracted products from reactants. ΔS° = Σ S°(products) − Σ S°(reactants).

items.q: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes: 2 H₂O₂(l) → 2 H₂O(l) + O₂(g). S° values in J/(mol·K): H₂O₂(l) 109.6, H₂O(l) 69.9, O₂(g) 205.2. Calculate ΔS°.

mistakes.why: Value: you left out the coefficients of 2 on H₂O₂ and H₂O.

items.q: A student calculates ΔS° = +38.4 J/(mol·K) for 2 SO₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2 SO₃(g). Without redoing the arithmetic, why should the student doubt this result?
options: SO₃ is a heavier molecule than SO₂, so ΔS° should be zero.
Combination reactions release heat, so ΔS° should be larger than +38.4.
ΔS° values are given in kJ, so a value as large as 38.4 is impossible.
Three moles of gas become two, so ΔS° should be negative.

items.q: For which reaction is it hardest to predict the sign of ΔS° without a table of S° values?
options: 2 H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2 H₂O(g)
H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2 HCl(g)
NH₄Cl(s) → NH₃(g) + HCl(g)
C₃H₈(g) + 5 O₂(g) → 3 CO₂(g) + 4 H₂O(g)

items.q: A reaction has ΔS° = −120 J/(mol·K). A student needs this value in the same energy unit as ΔH° = −92 kJ/mol. What is ΔS° in that unit?
options: −1.20 kJ/(mol·K)
−393 kJ/(mol·K)

items.q: Which process is thermodynamically favored at every temperature?
options: Q
P
R
S

items.q: Which processes are thermodynamically favored at 298 K? Select ALL that apply.
options: P
Q
R
S

items.q: Above what temperature does process R become thermodynamically favored?

mistakes.why: Value: you divided kJ by J. Convert ΔH° to 58,400 J/mol (or ΔS° to 0.152 kJ/(mol·K)) first.
Units: T = ΔH°/ΔS° gives kelvin. 384 K is 111 °C; the question asks for the temperature in K.

items.q: Calculate ΔG° for process R at 500. K.

mistakes.why: Value: you used ΔS° in J/(mol·K) with ΔH° in kJ/mol. Convert 152 J/(mol·K) to 0.152 kJ/(mol·K).
Value: you used 227 °C instead of 500. K. The temperature is already in kelvin.
Sign: ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°; subtract TΔS°.

items.q: Process Q is carried out at higher and higher temperatures. What happens to whether it is favored, and why?
options: It becomes more favored, because a higher temperature speeds up the reaction.
It stays favored as T rises, because it is an exothermic process.
It stops being favored above about 0.770 K, where ΔH° and ΔS° are equal.
It stops being favored above about 770 K, where the positive −TΔS° outweighs ΔH°.

items.q: Use the graph to find ΔH° for the reaction.

mistakes.why: Value: 600 is where the line crosses zero, a temperature in K. ΔH° is the value of ΔG° where T = 0.

items.q: Use the slope of the graph to find ΔS° for the reaction, in J/(mol·K).

mistakes.why: Sign: the slope is −ΔS°. A line that falls as T rises means ΔS° is positive.
Value: 0.150 is the slope in kJ/(mol·K). The question asks for J/(mol·K): multiply by 1000.

items.q: In which temperature range is the decomposition thermodynamically favored?
options: Above 600 K, where the line is below zero
Below 600 K, where the line is above zero
At exactly 600 K, where ΔG° is zero
Across the whole range shown, since the reaction absorbs heat

items.q: Which particle-level reasoning explains why ΔS° for this reaction is positive?
options: The products are more disordered because there are two of them instead of one.
Heat is absorbed, so the solid products have more energy than the reactant.
A gas forms from a solid, so Z particles spread through the container: more arrangements.
Breaking X apart releases energy, and released energy spreads out.

items.q: For N₂(g) + 3 H₂(g) → 2 NH₃(g), ΔH° = −92.2 kJ/mol and ΔS° = −198.1 J/(mol·K). Calculate ΔG° at 298 K.

mistakes.why: Value: you combined kJ with J. Convert ΔS° to −0.1981 kJ/(mol·K) before multiplying by T.
Value: you used 25 °C. T must be in kelvin: 298 K.
Sign: ΔS° is negative, so −TΔS° = −(298)(−0.1981) = +59.0 kJ/mol.

items.q: For CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g), ΔH° = +178.3 kJ/mol and ΔS° = +160.2 J/(mol·K). Calculate the lowest temperature at which the reaction is thermodynamically favored.

mistakes.why: Units: T = ΔH°/ΔS° comes out in kelvin. Report it in K.

items.q: Calculate ΔG° for C₂H₅OH(l) + 3 O₂(g) → 2 CO₂(g) + 3 H₂O(l). Standard free energies of formation, ΔG°f, in kJ/mol: C₂H₅OH(l) −174.8, CO₂(g) −394.4, H₂O(l) −237.1.

mistakes.why: Value: you left out the coefficients 2 on CO₂ and 3 on H₂O.
Sign: subtract the reactant term: − (−174.8) = +174.8.

items.q: For ice melting, ΔH° = +6.01 kJ/mol and ΔS° = +22.0 J/(mol·K). Which statement about a block of ice at −10 °C (263 K) is supported by these data?
options: It melts: ΔS° is positive, and any process with a positive ΔS° is favored.
It melts: ΔG° = 6.01 − (−10)(0.0220) = +6.23 kJ/mol, which is close to zero.
It does not melt: ΔG° = 6.01 − 263(0.0220) = +0.22 kJ/mol, so melting is not favored.
It does not melt: melting absorbs heat, and heat-absorbing processes are not favored.

items.q: Solid ammonium nitrate dissolves readily in water at 25 °C even though the solution gets colder. Which is the best explanation?
options: ΔH° > 0, but the ions spreading out make ΔS° large, so TΔS° > ΔH° and ΔG° < 0.
ΔH° < 0, because the solution gets colder as heat is released from it, so ΔG° < 0.
A process that happens on its own is exothermic, so dissolving releases heat here as well.
ΔG° > 0, but the salt dissolves anyway because water is a strong solvent.

items.q: A student writes: "This reaction is endothermic, so it is favorable at all temperatures because it takes in energy." Which correction is accurate?
options: An endothermic reaction is not favored at any temperature, because it needs a supply of heat.
The student is right as long as ΔS° is negative, since both terms then point the same way.
Favorability depends on ΔH° alone, so the student needs to check its size.
An endothermic reaction is favored when TΔS° > ΔH°: ΔS° > 0 and a high enough T.

items.q: A reaction has ΔH° = −50.0 kJ/mol and ΔS° = −100. J/(mol·K). A student calculates ΔG° at 300. K as −50.0 − (300.)(−100.) = +29,950 kJ/mol. What went wrong?
options: The temperature should be in °C, so T = 27 and ΔG° = −47.3 kJ/mol instead.
ΔS° was not converted to kJ/(mol·K); with −0.100 kJ/(mol·K), ΔG° = −20.0 kJ/mol.
The sign of ΔS° should have been ignored, giving ΔG° = −80.0 kJ/mol.
ΔH° should have been multiplied by T, giving ΔG° = −15,000 kJ/mol.

items.q: Which reactions in the table are thermodynamically favored at 298 K?
options: Reaction 2 alone, because it is the one that is observed
All three
Reactions 2 and 3, because their ΔG° values are large
No reaction in the table, because two show no change

items.q: Which statement best explains why Reaction 3 shows no change in an hour?
options: Its ΔG° is positive at 298 K, so the mixture has to be heated before water can form.
The mixture is already at equilibrium, so no further change can occur.
The reaction absorbs too much heat from the surroundings to proceed.
Its activation energy is large, so few H₂–O₂ collisions have enough energy to react.

items.q: A spark is passed through the mixture in Reaction 3 and it reacts explosively. What does the spark do?
options: It gets some molecules over the barrier; the heat they release lets others react.
It changes ΔG° from positive to negative, which makes the reaction favored.
It lowers the activation energy permanently, the way a catalyst does.
It shifts the equilibrium constant to favor products for as long as the spark lasts.

items.q: Diamonds kept for centuries do not turn into graphite. Which statement is correct?
options: Diamond is thermodynamically more stable than graphite at 298 K.
The conversion is not favored, because its ΔG° is small.
Diamond is kinetically stable: the change is favored but has a huge Ea.
The conversion is at equilibrium, so equal amounts of diamond and graphite are present.

items.q: Which product is thermodynamically favored more strongly?
options: B, because its barrier is lower
B, because it is the product that forms first
C, because its ΔG° is more negative
Neither, because both reactions are endothermic

items.q: At 25 °C, A is mostly converted to B within minutes, and almost no C forms in that time. Which explanation is best?
options: The barrier to B is much lower, so many more collisions reach B: kinetic control.
B is thermodynamically more stable than C, so the reaction stops at B.
C does not form, because a barrier of 110 kJ/mol is impossible to cross at 25 °C.
B forms because its ΔG° is closer to zero, so less energy has to be released.

items.q: A chemist wants mostly C. Which change is most likely to help, and why?
options: Cool the mixture, because a lower temperature favors the product with the larger barrier.
Stop the reaction after a few minutes, before C has had a chance to break down.
Add more A, because a higher concentration lowers the activation energy for C.
Heat it for a long time, so collisions can cross the larger barrier to C.

items.q: Which statement compares the two pathways correctly?
options: Formation of B is faster and more favored.
Formation of B is faster; formation of C is more favored.
Formation of C is faster and more favored.
The two pathways have the same rate, because they start from the same compound.

items.q: What does a negative ΔG° tell you about a reaction?
options: It is favored, but it may be fast or very slow.
It will happen quickly once the reactants are mixed.
It has a small activation energy barrier.
It needs a continuous input of energy to keep going.

items.q: Paper burns in air with ΔG° far below zero, yet a book can sit on a shelf for a hundred years. Which explanation is best?
options: ΔG° for burning paper becomes positive at room temperature.
Paper is at equilibrium with the oxygen in the air.
Burning paper has a large Ea, so at 25 °C its rate is negligible.
There is not enough oxygen in the air for the reaction to be favored.

items.q: Adding a catalyst to a reaction that is under kinetic control has which effect?
options: It makes ΔG° more negative, so the reaction becomes more favored.
It lowers Ea so the reaction can run at a measurable rate; ΔG° stays the same.
It makes a reaction with ΔG° > 0 favored.
It raises the activation energy of the reverse reaction alone, so products build up.

items.q: A student mixes two solutions, sees no reaction after an hour, and concludes "ΔG° for this reaction must be positive." Which reply is best?
options: That is correct, because any reaction with ΔG° < 0 happens within minutes.
That is correct, because a reaction that does not happen has ΔG° = 0.
That does not follow, because ΔG° is negative for any reaction that releases heat.
It does not follow: a favored reaction can be too slow to see; ΔG° comes from data.

items.q: Which are examples of a thermodynamically favored process that is under kinetic control at room temperature? Select ALL that apply.
options: Methane and oxygen in a gas stove before it is lit
An iron nail that rusts only over months
Ice melting on a kitchen counter at 25 °C
Water decomposing into hydrogen and oxygen in a closed bottle

items.q: Glucose and oxygen react with ΔG° = −2870 kJ/mol, yet sugar in a bowl does not burn. In your cells, enzymes let the same overall reaction run at body temperature. What do the enzymes change?
options: The sign of ΔG°, so the reaction becomes favored in the body
The products of the reaction, so less energy is released
The temperature of the cell, so it reaches the burning point of sugar
The activation energy of each step, so it runs at a useful rate

items.q: Which pair of data would show that a reaction at 298 K is under kinetic control?
options: ΔG° = +40 kJ/mol and no measurable product after a week
ΔG° = −150 kJ/mol and no measurable product after a week
ΔG° = −150 kJ/mol and a complete reaction within one second
ΔG° = +40 kJ/mol and complete reaction in one second

items.q: Calculate K for reaction A at 298 K.

mistakes.why: Value: you used ΔG° in kJ with R in J. Convert −20.0 kJ/mol to −20,000 J/mol.
Value: you raised 10 to the power instead of e. ΔG° = −RT ln K uses the natural log, so K = e^(−ΔG°/RT).
Sign: −ΔG°/RT = −(−20,000)/(8.314 × 298) = +8.07, a positive exponent, so K > 1.

items.q: At equilibrium, which reaction has mostly reactants and very little product?
options: A

items.q: A student says reaction D, with ΔG° = +5.0 kJ/mol, "cannot happen at all." Which reply is best?
options: K ≈ 0.13, so from pure reactants some product forms until Q = K.
The student is right, because a reaction with ΔG° > 0 makes no product.
The reaction goes to completion, because ΔG° is so close to zero.
The reaction happens once a catalyst is added, which makes ΔG° negative.

items.q: Calculate ΔG° for the ionization of acetic acid at 298 K.

mistakes.why: Value: you used log instead of ln. ΔG° = −RT ln K uses the natural log.
Sign: ln(1.8 × 10⁻⁵) is negative, so −RT ln K is positive.
Units: R in J/(mol·K) gives J/mol. Divide by 1000 to report kJ/mol.

items.q: Which equilibrium has a negative ΔG°?
options: The ionization of acetic acid
The dissociation of N₂O₄
The formation of NH₃
No equilibrium in the table, since at equilibrium ΔG° = 0

items.q: Using the K value in the table, calculate ΔG° at 298 K for the reverse of the N₂O₄ dissociation: 2 NO₂(g) ⇌ N₂O₄(g).

mistakes.why: Sign: this is the reverse of the reaction in the table, so K = 1/0.15 = 6.7 and ΔG° is negative.

items.q: A flask of N₂O₄ and NO₂ at 298 K has Q = 0.010. Which statement is correct?
options: ΔG° is positive, so NO₂ can form after the flask is heated, not before.
Q < K, so the net reaction forms more N₂O₄ until Q rises to K.
Q < K, so ΔG is negative now and the net reaction forms more NO₂.
K changes to 0.010 to match the flask, so there is no net reaction.

items.q: For N₂(g) + 3 H₂(g) ⇌ 2 NH₃(g), ΔG° = −33.2 kJ/mol at 298 K. Calculate K. (R = 8.314 J/(mol·K))

mistakes.why: Value: ΔG° must be in J/mol to match R: −33,200 J/mol.
Sign: −ΔG°/RT = +13.4, so K is large, not small.

items.q: A gas-phase reaction has K = 20.2 at 400. K. Calculate ΔG° at 400. K, in kJ/mol.

mistakes.why: Value: you used 298 K. Use the temperature at which K was measured: 400. K.
Value: 400. K is already in kelvin; do not subtract 273.
Value: use ln, not log, in ΔG° = −RT ln K.

items.q: If ΔG° for a reaction is large and negative, what is true of K?
options: K is much greater than 1, so products are favored at equilibrium.
K is much less than 1, so reactants are favored at equilibrium.
K is equal to 1, so equal amounts of reactants and products are present.
K is negative, because ΔG° is negative.

items.q: Reaction 1 has ΔG° = −5.70 kJ/mol and K₁ = 9.98 at 298 K. Reaction 2 is reaction 1 multiplied by 2. What are ΔG° and K for reaction 2?
options: ΔG° = −11.4 kJ/mol and K = 20.0
ΔG° = −5.70 kJ/mol and K = 99.6
ΔG° = −2.85 kJ/mol and K = 3.16
ΔG° = −11.4 kJ/mol and K = 99.6

items.q: A reaction mixture is at equilibrium. Which statement is correct?
options: ΔG° is zero, because nothing in the mixture is changing.
ΔG for the system is zero, while ΔG° keeps its fixed value set by K.
ΔG is negative, because the forward reaction is still running.
K equals zero, because the reaction has stopped.

items.q: For a reaction at 298 K, ΔG° = +0.5 kJ/mol. Which description of the equilibrium mixture is best?
options: K ≈ 0.8, close to 1, so both reactants and products are abundant.
K is very small, so the mixture is nearly pure reactants.
K is very large, so the reaction goes nearly to completion.
K is 0.5, the same number as ΔG° in kJ/mol.

items.q: NH₄NO₃ dissolves readily in water and the water gets colder. Which statement explains both observations?
options: The ions release energy as water molecules surround them, which makes ΔH° negative and ΔG° negative.
ΔH°soln > 0, so the water cools, but the ions spreading out makes TΔS° > ΔH°.
The water gets colder because ΔS° is negative, and a negative ΔS° makes ΔG° negative.
Dissolving is a physical change, so ΔG° does not apply and the salt dissolves because it is ionic.

items.q: Which salt’s dissolving is favored mainly because of the enthalpy change, even though the entropy change works against it?
options: NH₄NO₃
NaCl
Salt Z
CaCl₂

items.q: Salt Z has small, doubly charged ions. Which explanation of its negative ΔS°soln is best?
options: Each small, highly charged ion holds water tightly; that water’s lost freedom outweighs the ions’ spreading.
The ions of Salt Z stay in the crystal, so they do not disperse through the water.
The solution is more disordered than the solid, which makes ΔS° negative.
Dissolving Salt Z releases heat, and releasing heat lowers the entropy of the solution.

items.q: Calculate ΔG°soln for Salt Z at 298 K.

items.q: Is the orientation of the water molecules in the drawing correct?

items.q: Forming the attractions shown in the drawing has which energy effect?
options: It absorbs energy, because water has to be pulled toward the ions.
It has no energy effect, because no chemical bonds form.
It releases energy, as opposite partial charges come together.
It absorbs energy, because the ions break apart from the crystal at that moment.

items.q: The ion-dipole attractions in the drawing are stronger for Mg²⁺ than for Na⁺. Which is the best explanation?
options: Mg²⁺ has a larger charge and smaller radius, so its Coulombic attraction is greater.
Mg²⁺ has a larger molar mass, so it attracts water more strongly.
Mg²⁺ has more electrons than Na⁺, so it is more polarizable.
Mg²⁺ forms covalent bonds with water, while Na⁺ forms ionic bonds.

items.q: How does the ordering of water shown in the drawing affect ΔS°soln?
options: It raises ΔS°soln, because water molecules move in closer to the ions.
It has no effect on ΔS°soln, because the water was already a liquid.
It raises ΔS°soln, because ion-dipole attractions release heat.
It lowers ΔS°soln: water held around ions has fewer arrangements.

items.q: Which step in dissolving an ionic solid releases energy?
options: Separating the ions of the crystal from one another
Water molecules surrounding the separated ions
Separating water molecules to make room for the ions
Heating the water before the solid is added

items.q: When salt Q dissolves in water, the solution warms up. Which conclusion about the steps of dissolving is supported?
options: Forming ion-dipole attractions releases more energy than separating ions and water absorbs.
Separating the ions releases more energy than forming ion-dipole attractions absorbs.
No energy is absorbed in any step, because the solution warms up.
ΔS°soln is negative, which is why the solution gets warmer.

items.q: For a salt, ΔH°soln = +15 kJ/mol and ΔS°soln = +40 J/(mol·K). How does its solubility change as the water is heated from 298 K to 373 K?
options: It decreases: ΔH°soln is positive, so heating pushes the salt out of solution.
It does not change: solubility depends on the salt, not on temperature.
It increases: TΔS° grows, so ΔG°soln falls from +3.1 to +0.1 kJ/mol.
It increases: heating makes ΔH°soln negative.

items.q: A slightly soluble salt has ΔG°soln = +30.0 kJ/mol at 298 K. Calculate its Ksp. (R = 8.314 J/(mol·K))

Value: Ksp = e^(−ΔG°/RT), not 10^(−ΔG°/RT).

Silver chloride barely dissolving in water
Sugar dissolving faster in hot tea than in iced tea

A higher temperature of the water
